title: Bridging the Perimenopause Information Gap
summary: Women are done being quiet about perimenopause. While perimenopause has become less stigmatized in culture and media, most women are navigating the transition without the information or support they need. Hers can help. Hear from Jessica Shepherd, MD, MBA, FACOG, and Chief Medical Officer of Hers.
body_markdown:
It's not just your group chat. When Gabrielle Union told[People](https://people.com/gabrielle-union-felt-defective-due-to-perimenopause-symptoms-exclusive-8403678?_gl=1*1jigtbn*_ga*MTk3MzcxMzgwOS4xNzg3NjI0MzEz*_ga_DK3GDWHWJH*czE3ODc2MjQzMTMkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODc2MjQzNzIkajEkbDAkaDA.) she felt "defective" because of her perimenopause symptoms, or when Tracee Ellis Ross said the[transition](https://www.harpersbazaar.com/culture/features/a38058623/tracee-ellis-ross-interview-november-2021/) was "frying her brain," they were putting words to something I hear from patients every day. Even Amy Poehler’s[comment](https://www.buzzfeed.com/leylamohammed/jennifer-lawrence-stunned-amy-poehler-perimenopause-comment) to Jennifer Lawrence on her *Good Hang* podcast, that itchy ears can be a sign of perimenopause, went viral for how many women saw themselves in Lawrence's stunned reaction.


Perimenopause is a topic that women are done being quiet about. And while it’s heartening to see perimenopause become less stigmatized in culture and media, most women are navigating this transition without the information or support they need.


[More than two million women](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12014197/) in the U.S. begin perimenopause every year, and[more than half](https://menopause.org/wp-content/uploads/press-release/MENO-D-25-00558.pdf) can't tell it apart from stress, aging, or simple exhaustion. Even among women 40 to 44, the age when perimenopause most often begins,[42% don't know](https://menopause.org/wp-content/uploads/press-release/MENO-D-25-00558.pdf) which reproductive stage they're in. At the same time,[more women are having children later](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nvsr/nvsr74/nvsr74-1.pdf) in life: births to women 35 to 39 are up 90% since 1990, and in 2023, more babies were born to women 40 and older than to teenagers for the first time. That means postpartum and perimenopause are increasingly overlapping, often with no one around to help tell the two apart.


There's no test that can confirm perimenopause, which makes it easy for doctors to wave it away and easy for women to second-guess themselves right when they need answers most. Because of that, women are turning to other sources for information. Sixty six percent (66%) of women get health[information](https://www.pewresearch.org/science/2026/04/07/users-of-social-media-and-ai-chatbots-for-health-information-are-more-likely-to-say-they-are-convenient-than-accurate/) from social media and 40% turn to AI chatbots, even though few call what they find highly accurate.


What's left is a compounding information gap – women don't know what's happening to their bodies, and unreliable sources fill in the blanks with answers that sound confident but rarely hold up. Helping women through this transition should be grounded in ongoing care, not just a diagnosis.


##### **The Role of a Digital Health Partner.**


Digital experiences have already rewired how we shop, bank, and date. Healthcare is one of the last places to catch up. For women in perimenopause, a single appointment can give them a snapshot, but the reality is this transition changes month to month, which is why there is real value in a provider relationship that grows and evolves with you and your health journey instead of ending when the visit does


Through Hers, you can find individualized care without the traditional hurdles. In partnership with licensed providers and a care team trained in women’s health, women are able to access 24/7 care that is personalized to them. And the Hers app is full of content crafted by clinical experts in psychology, nutrition, exercise, sleep, and more to help set women up for success when navigating this transition.


Treatments like estrogen patches have faced[supply issues](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/patients-scramble-find-estrogen-patches-shortage-worsens-after-us-fda-champions-2026-04-09/) industry-wide this year, which is exactly why having a care partner who's actually paying attention matters. At Hers, we've strived to keep access to these treatments consistent even when supply has been depleted elsewhere, so no woman is left scrambling to find medication somewhere else.


{inline-gallery}


##### **The Next Chapter.**


Hormone replacement therapies, like estrogen and progesterone, are still the treatments most people associate with this stage of life. They work by replacing hormones that naturally decline as women age. Treatment plans through Hers can address hot flashes, night sweats, sleep disruption, mood changes, and vaginal dryness.


Hormone health is ever changing, as is every woman. The field is moving fast and we're paying close attention to where it's headed.
